entries.docTitle: Rainfall: measurement, categories and what the numbers mean
entries.heading: Rainfall: measurement, categories and what the numbers mean
entries.source: India Meteorological Department rainfall classification and WMO observation guidance (public documentation)
entries.text: > Source: India Meteorological Department rainfall classification and WMO observation guidance (public documentation)

entries.docTitle: Rainfall: measurement, categories and what the numbers mean
entries.heading: How rainfall is measured
entries.source: India Meteorological Department rainfall classification and WMO observation guidance (public documentation)
entries.text: Rainfall is measured as the depth of water that would collect on a flat surface if nothing drained or evaporated, reported in millimetres (mm). One millimetre of rain equals one litre of water per square metre. A rain gauge collects rainfall over a fixed period, usually 24 hours, from 08:30 IST to 08:30 IST in India.

entries.docTitle: Rainfall: measurement, categories and what the numbers mean
entries.heading: Daily rainfall categories used in India
entries.source: India Meteorological Department rainfall classification and WMO observation guidance (public documentation)
entries.text:
The India Meteorological Department groups 24-hour station rainfall into standard categories:

- Very light rain: 0.1 mm to 2.4 mm
- Light rain: 2.5 mm to 15.5 mm
- Moderate rain: 15.6 mm to 64.4 mm
- Heavy rain: 64.5 mm to 115.5 mm
- Very heavy rain: 115.6 mm to 204.4 mm
- Extremely heavy rain: more than 204.4 mm

These thresholds matter because urban drainage systems are usually designed for moderate rainfall. Once totals cross the heavy category, waterlogging and traffic disruption become likely even in well-drained cities.

entries.docTitle: Rainfall: measurement, categories and what the numbers mean
entries.heading: Rain probability versus rainfall amount
entries.source: India Meteorological Department rainfall classification and WMO observation guidance (public documentation)
entries.text: Probability of precipitation is the chance that measurable rain (at least 0.1 mm) falls at a given point during a given hour or day. It says nothing about intensity. A 90% probability with 1 mm forecast means a near-certain drizzle. A 40% probability with 50 mm forecast means rain is less likely, but heavy if it arrives. Always read the two numbers together.

entries.docTitle: Rainfall: measurement, categories and what the numbers mean
entries.heading: Rainfall intensity
entries.source: India Meteorological Department rainfall classification and WMO observation guidance (public documentation)
entries.text: Intensity is depth per hour. Short bursts above roughly 10 mm per hour overwhelm most storm drains and are the usual cause of flash urban flooding, even when the daily total looks unremarkable.

entries.heading: Heavy rainfall and urban flooding
entries.source: National Disaster Management Authority (India) urban flooding guidelines, public guidance
entries.text: > Source: National Disaster Management Authority (India) urban flooding guidelines, public guidance

entries.heading: Why cities flood
entries.source: National Disaster Management Authority (India) urban flooding guidelines, public guidance
entries.text: Urban flooding happens when rainfall exceeds the capacity of drains, or when drains are blocked by silt and solid waste. Paved surfaces prevent infiltration, so a much larger share of rainfall becomes surface runoff than in rural areas. Flooding can therefore occur within minutes of intense rain beginning, and can happen far from any river.

entries.heading: Warning signs
entries.source: National Disaster Management Authority (India) urban flooding guidelines, public guidance
entries.text: Rapidly rising water in streets, water backing up from drains, sustained rainfall over several hours, and upstream rainfall in the catchment even when it is dry locally.

entries.heading: Safety actions before heavy rain
entries.source: National Disaster Management Authority (India) urban flooding guidelines, public guidance
entries.text:
- Charge phones and power banks, and keep a torch accessible.
- Store drinking water, since supply and treatment can be disrupted.
- Move vehicles out of basements and low-lying parking.
- Keep important documents in a waterproof bag on an upper shelf.
- Identify the nearest higher ground and the safest route to it.

entries.heading: During flooding
entries.source: National Disaster Management Authority (India) urban flooding guidelines, public guidance
entries.text: Do not walk or drive through moving water. About 15 cm of moving water can knock an adult off balance, and about 60 cm can float most cars. Floodwater hides open manholes, live cables and debris. Avoid contact with electrical fittings if water has entered the building, and switch off the mains at the board if it is safe and dry to reach.

entries.heading: After flooding
entries.source: National Disaster Management Authority (India) urban flooding guidelines, public guidance
entries.text: Assume floodwater is contaminated. Boil or disinfect drinking water until authorities confirm supply is safe, discard soaked food, and get electrical wiring checked before switching supply back on. Watch for waterborne illness in the days that follow.

entries.heading: Thunderstorms and lightning safety
entries.source: WMO and National Disaster Management Authority (India) lightning safety guidance, public documentation
entries.text: > Source: WMO and National Disaster Management Authority (India) lightning safety guidance, public documentation

entries.heading: How thunderstorms form
entries.source: WMO and National Disaster Management Authority (India) lightning safety guidance, public documentation
entries.text: Thunderstorms need moisture, an unstable atmosphere where air keeps rising, and a trigger such as daytime heating or a front. Rapidly rising moist air builds a cumulonimbus cloud, and charge separation inside the cloud produces lightning. Most single-cell storms last under an hour, but severe storms can persist much longer and produce hail, sudden wind gusts and intense rain.

entries.heading: The 30/30 rule
entries.source: WMO and National Disaster Management Authority (India) lightning safety guidance, public documentation
entries.text: If the gap between a lightning flash and its thunder is less than 30 seconds, the strike is within about 10 km and close enough to be dangerous: move indoors immediately. Stay inside for 30 minutes after the last thunder, because strikes often occur at the trailing edge of a storm under apparently clearing skies.

entries.heading: Safe and unsafe places
entries.source: WMO and National Disaster Management Authority (India) lightning safety guidance, public documentation
entries.text: Safe: a fully enclosed building with wiring and plumbing, or a hard-topped vehicle with windows closed. Unsafe: open fields, hilltops, beaches, isolated trees, bus shelters, verandahs, metal sheds, and anywhere near tall metal objects.

entries.heading: Indoors during a storm
entries.source: WMO and National Disaster Management Authority (India) lightning safety guidance, public documentation
entries.text: Avoid corded phones, plumbing and direct contact with concrete walls or floors that contain metal reinforcement. Unplug sensitive electronics before the storm arrives rather than during it.

entries.heading: Lightning risk in agriculture
entries.source: WMO and National Disaster Management Authority (India) lightning safety guidance, public documentation
entries.text: Farm workers in open fields are among the most affected groups in India. Where a storm is forecast, plan field work for earlier in the day and identify a solid shelter before starting.

entries.heading: Heat, heatwaves and heat illness
entries.source: India Meteorological Department heatwave criteria and World Health Organization heat-health guidance, public documentation
entries.text: > Source: India Meteorological Department heatwave criteria and World Health Organization heat-health guidance, public documentation

entries.heading: How a heatwave is declared in India
entries.source: India Meteorological Department heatwave criteria and World Health Organization heat-health guidance, public documentation
entries.text: IMD declares a heatwave for plains when the maximum temperature reaches at least 40°C and is 4.5°C to 6.4°C above the normal for that place and date; a severe heatwave when the departure exceeds 6.4°C. A heatwave is also declared when the actual maximum reaches 45°C, and a severe heatwave at 47°C, regardless of departure. Thresholds are lower for hilly and coastal areas.

entries.heading: Why humidity matters
entries.source: India Meteorological Department heatwave criteria and World Health Organization heat-health guidance, public documentation
entries.text: The body cools mainly by evaporating sweat. High humidity slows evaporation, so 36°C with very high humidity can stress the body more than 40°C in dry air. "Feels like" or apparent temperature combines air temperature, humidity and wind to describe this.

entries.heading: Recognising heat illness
entries.source: India Meteorological Department heatwave criteria and World Health Organization heat-health guidance, public documentation
entries.text:
- Heat cramps: painful muscle spasms, heavy sweating.
- Heat exhaustion: heavy sweating, weakness, nausea, headache, cool clammy skin, fast weak pulse. Move to a cool place, loosen clothing, sip water, apply cool wet cloths.
- Heat stroke: body temperature above about 40°C, hot skin that may be dry, confusion or unconsciousness. This is a medical emergency. Call for help, move the person to shade and cool them aggressively with water while waiting.

entries.heading: Reducing risk
entries.source: India Meteorological Department heatwave criteria and World Health Organization heat-health guidance, public documentation
entries.text: Drink water before feeling thirsty, avoid direct sun between 11:00 and 16:00, wear light loose cotton clothing, and reschedule strenuous outdoor work. Infants, people over 65, pregnant women, outdoor workers and people with chronic illness are at higher risk. Never leave children or pets in parked vehicles.

entries.heading: Wind speed, gusts and safety
entries.source: Beaufort wind scale (WMO) and general public-safety guidance
entries.text: > Source: Beaufort wind scale (WMO) and general public-safety guidance

entries.heading: Sustained wind versus gusts
entries.source: Beaufort wind scale (WMO) and general public-safety guidance
entries.text: Sustained wind is an average over a period, usually ten minutes. A gust is a brief peak, typically lasting seconds. Damage usually tracks gust speed rather than the average, so forecasts report both.

entries.heading: What wind speeds feel like
entries.source: Beaufort wind scale (WMO) and general public-safety guidance
entries.text:
- 20 to 38 km/h: leaves and small branches move; dust is raised.
- 39 to 61 km/h: whole trees sway; walking against the wind is difficult.
- 62 to 88 km/h: twigs break off trees; light structural damage begins; two-wheeler travel becomes risky.
- 89 to 117 km/h: trees uproot, hoardings and roofing sheets fail.
- Above 118 km/h: hurricane force on the Beaufort scale, with widespread damage.

entries.heading: Practical precautions
entries.source: Beaufort wind scale (WMO) and general public-safety guidance
entries.text: Secure or bring in loose items such as flower pots, signage and drying racks. Park away from old trees, scaffolding and advertising hoardings. Close and latch windows on the windward side. On the road, hold the steering wheel firmly when passing gaps between buildings or crossing bridges and flyovers, where crosswinds are strongest.

entries.heading: Squalls and sudden gusts
entries.source: Beaufort wind scale (WMO) and general public-safety guidance
entries.text: A squall is a sudden increase in wind speed lasting several minutes, often just ahead of a thunderstorm. Squall gusts can arrive before any rain, which is why outdoor structures and tents fail unexpectedly at the start of a storm.

entries.heading: Tropical cyclones
entries.source: India Meteorological Department cyclone classification and NDMA cyclone preparedness guidance, public documentation
entries.text: > Source: India Meteorological Department cyclone classification and NDMA cyclone preparedness guidance, public documentation

entries.heading: Classification used in the North Indian Ocean
entries.source: India Meteorological Department cyclone classification and NDMA cyclone preparedness guidance, public documentation
entries.text:
IMD classifies systems by maximum sustained surface wind:

- Depression: 31 to 49 km/h
- Deep depression: 50 to 61 km/h
- Cyclonic storm: 62 to 88 km/h
- Severe cyclonic storm: 89 to 117 km/h
- Very severe cyclonic storm: 118 to 166 km/h
- Extremely severe cyclonic storm: 167 to 221 km/h
- Super cyclonic storm: 222 km/h and above

entries.heading: The main hazards
entries.source: India Meteorological Department cyclone classification and NDMA cyclone preparedness guidance, public documentation
entries.text: Storm surge, the rise of seawater pushed ashore by wind and low pressure, causes most cyclone deaths. Other hazards are destructive wind, very heavy rain and inland flooding, which can occur hundreds of kilometres from the landfall point.

entries.heading: Warning stages in India
entries.source: India Meteorological Department cyclone classification and NDMA cyclone preparedness guidance, public documentation
entries.text: IMD issues staged bulletins as a system approaches: pre-cyclone watch, cyclone alert, cyclone warning and post-landfall outlook, with increasing lead time detail. Coastal districts operate cyclone shelters and evacuation plans based on these bulletins.

entries.heading: Preparing
entries.source: India Meteorological Department cyclone classification and NDMA cyclone preparedness guidance, public documentation
entries.text: Know whether your area is in an evacuation zone, keep an emergency kit with water, food, medicines, documents and a torch, and keep a battery radio for when networks fail. Evacuate when told to, before conditions deteriorate. The calm during the eye of a cyclone is temporary and is followed by winds from the opposite direction.

entries.heading: Flood safety
entries.source: National Disaster Management Authority (India) flood guidance, public documentation
entries.text: > Source: National Disaster Management Authority (India) flood guidance, public documentation

entries.heading: Types of flooding
entries.source: National Disaster Management Authority (India) flood guidance, public documentation
entries.text: River or riverine flooding builds over hours to days as a catchment drains. Flash flooding develops within minutes to a few hours from intense rain, dam or embankment failure, or cloudbursts, and is the most dangerous because there is little warning. Coastal flooding comes from storm surge and high tides.

entries.heading: Key rule
entries.source: National Disaster Management Authority (India) flood guidance, public documentation
entries.text: Turn around, do not drown. Never enter moving water on foot or in a vehicle. Depth is impossible to judge, roads may be washed away beneath the surface, and water rises faster than most people expect.

entries.heading: If a flood warning is issued
entries.source: National Disaster Management Authority (India) flood guidance, public documentation
entries.text: Move livestock, vehicles and valuables to higher ground early. Switch off electricity and gas at the mains if water is likely to enter. Keep documents, medicines and a phone charger in a grab bag. Follow the evacuation route advised by local authorities rather than a familiar shortcut that may be submerged.

entries.heading: If trapped by rising water
entries.source: National Disaster Management Authority (India) flood guidance, public documentation
entries.text: Move to the highest floor but avoid a sealed attic where you could be trapped by rising water. Signal for help from a window or roof. Keep a whistle and a torch with you.

entries.heading: Health after a flood
entries.source: National Disaster Management Authority (India) flood guidance, public documentation
entries.text: Floodwater mixes with sewage, chemicals and debris. Wash hands before eating, boil drinking water until supply is declared safe, treat cuts promptly, and watch for fever or diarrhoea. Snakebite and electrocution risks rise during cleanup.

entries.heading: Humidity, dew point and comfort
entries.source: WMO Guide to Meteorological Instruments and Methods of Observation, general meteorological reference
entries.text: > Source: WMO Guide to Meteorological Instruments and Methods of Observation, general meteorological reference

entries.heading: Relative humidity
entries.source: WMO Guide to Meteorological Instruments and Methods of Observation, general meteorological reference
entries.text: Relative humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air as a percentage of the maximum the air can hold at that temperature. Because warm air holds more vapour, relative humidity falls during the day as temperature rises, even when the actual moisture content does not change. This is why morning readings are usually higher than afternoon readings.

entries.heading: Dew point
entries.source: WMO Guide to Meteorological Instruments and Methods of Observation, general meteorological reference
entries.text:
Dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated and condensation begins. Unlike relative humidity, it measures the absolute moisture in the air and is a better guide to how muggy conditions feel:

- Below 13°C: dry and comfortable
- 13 to 16°C: comfortable
- 16 to 20°C: becoming noticeable
- 20 to 24°C: humid and uncomfortable
- Above 24°C: oppressive, with reduced ability to cool by sweating

entries.heading: Why it matters for safety
entries.source: WMO Guide to Meteorological Instruments and Methods of Observation, general meteorological reference
entries.text: High humidity reduces evaporative cooling, raising heat stress at a given temperature. It also supports fog formation when temperatures drop overnight to near the dew point, and it is one of the ingredients thunderstorms need.

entries.heading: Fog and visibility
entries.source: WMO Guide to Meteorological Instruments and Methods of Observation, general meteorological reference
entries.text: When air cools to its dew point near the surface, fog forms. Radiation fog is common on clear calm nights, especially in winter over north India, and usually clears a few hours after sunrise. Visibility below 1000 metres is classified as fog; below 200 metres it seriously affects road, rail and air travel.

entries.heading: Atmospheric pressure and weather systems
entries.source: WMO and standard meteorological reference material
entries.text: > Source: WMO and standard meteorological reference material

entries.heading: What pressure measures
entries.source: WMO and standard meteorological reference material
entries.text: Atmospheric pressure is the weight of the air column above a point, reported in hectopascals (hPa). Mean sea level pressure averages about 1013 hPa. Values are corrected to sea level so that readings from different altitudes can be compared.

entries.heading: Highs and lows
entries.source: WMO and standard meteorological reference material
entries.text: In a low pressure area, air converges and rises, cools, and condenses, so lows are associated with clouds, rain and unsettled weather. In a high pressure area, air sinks and warms, which suppresses cloud formation and brings clearer, more settled weather.

entries.heading: Reading pressure changes
entries.source: WMO and standard meteorological reference material
entries.text: The trend matters more than the absolute value. A drop of 3 hPa or more in three hours often indicates an approaching or deepening system with strengthening wind. A steady rise usually means improving conditions. Rapid deep falls near the coast during the cyclone season are a serious sign.

entries.heading: Fronts
entries.source: WMO and standard meteorological reference material
entries.text: A front is the boundary between two air masses of different temperature and humidity. Fronts are the main driver of mid-latitude weather changes, producing bands of cloud and rain. In tropical India, day-to-day weather is driven more by the monsoon trough, low pressure systems over the Bay of Bengal, western disturbances in winter, and local convection than by classical fronts.

entries.heading: Monsoon systems
entries.source: WMO and standard meteorological reference material
entries.text: The southwest monsoon (June to September) and the northeast monsoon (October to December, affecting Tamil Nadu and adjoining regions) deliver most of India's annual rainfall, modulated by monsoon lows, depressions and active or break phases.

entries.heading: The UV index
entries.source: World Health Organization global solar UV index guidance, public documentation
entries.text: > Source: World Health Organization global solar UV index guidance, public documentation

entries.heading: What the index means
entries.source: World Health Organization global solar UV index guidance, public documentation
entries.text: The UV index describes the strength of ultraviolet radiation at the surface on an open scale starting at zero. It is highest near solar noon, increases with altitude, and is stronger at lower latitudes. Cloud cover reduces it only partly, and snow, sand and water reflect UV, raising exposure.

entries.heading: Categories and recommended protection
entries.source: World Health Organization global solar UV index guidance, public documentation
entries.text:
- 0 to 2 (low): no protection needed for most people.
- 3 to 5 (moderate): seek shade near midday, wear a hat and sunglasses, apply sunscreen.
- 6 to 7 (high): protection required; reduce time in the sun between 10:00 and 16:00.
- 8 to 10 (very high): extra protection; unprotected skin can burn quickly.
- 11 and above (extreme): avoid being outdoors during midday hours; take all precautions.

Most of India records very high to extreme values during clear days from March to June, particularly at midday.

entries.heading: Practical protection
entries.source: World Health Organization global solar UV index guidance, public documentation
entries.text: Use a broad-spectrum sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher and reapply every two hours and after sweating or swimming. Tightly woven clothing, a wide-brimmed hat and UV-blocking sunglasses give reliable protection. Shade is most effective in the hours around noon, when UV is at its peak.

entries.heading: Weather versus climate
entries.source: WMO and IPCC public explanatory material
entries.text: > Source: WMO and IPCC public explanatory material

entries.heading: The difference
entries.source: WMO and IPCC public explanatory material
entries.text: Weather is the state of the atmosphere over minutes to days: today's temperature, this evening's rain, tomorrow's wind. Climate is the statistical description of weather over long periods, conventionally 30 years, including averages, extremes and variability. A common summary is that climate is what you expect and weather is what you get.

entries.heading: Climate normals
entries.source: WMO and IPCC public explanatory material
entries.text: A climate normal is the average of a variable over a standard 30-year period, currently 1991 to 2020. Normals are the baseline used to say whether a month was warmer or wetter than usual, and they are how departures such as "4.5°C above normal" in heatwave criteria are defined.

entries.heading: Why a cold day does not disprove warming
entries.source: WMO and IPCC public explanatory material
entries.text: Climate statements describe long-term averages across large areas. Individual cold days, or a single wet month, are weather. Trends are assessed over decades and across many stations, and are separated from natural variability such as El Niño and La Niña using statistical methods.

entries.heading: Climate variability in India
entries.source: WMO and IPCC public explanatory material
entries.text: Year-to-year monsoon rainfall in India varies substantially, partly in response to sea surface temperature patterns in the Pacific and Indian Oceans. El Niño years are often, though not always, associated with weaker monsoon rainfall. Because of this variability, a single season is rarely evidence of a long-term trend.

entries.heading: How climate information is used
entries.source: WMO and IPCC public explanatory material
entries.text: Planners use climate statistics for drainage design, crop calendars, reservoir operation and heat action plans, while weather forecasts drive day-to-day decisions and disaster response.

entries.heading: How weather forecasts are made
entries.source: WMO guidance on numerical weather prediction, public documentation
entries.text: > Source: WMO guidance on numerical weather prediction, public documentation

entries.heading: Numerical weather prediction
entries.source: WMO guidance on numerical weather prediction, public documentation
entries.text: Forecasts start with observations from surface stations, weather balloons, aircraft, ships, buoys, radar and satellites. These are combined into a best estimate of the current atmosphere in a step called data assimilation. Physics equations describing motion, heat and moisture are then solved forward in time on a three-dimensional grid.

entries.heading: Why forecasts lose skill with time
entries.source: WMO guidance on numerical weather prediction, public documentation
entries.text: Small errors in the starting state grow, which limits useful detailed prediction to roughly a week to ten days. Forecast centres run ensembles, many slightly different simulations, to measure how confident a forecast is. When ensemble members agree, confidence is high; when they diverge, the forecast is uncertain and probabilities become more informative than single values.

entries.heading: Different models, different answers
entries.source: WMO guidance on numerical weather prediction, public documentation
entries.text: Major global models include ECMWF IFS from Europe, GFS from NOAA in the United States, and ICON from DWD in Germany. They differ in resolution, physics and assimilation, so they often disagree on the timing and placement of rainfall. Comparing models is a legitimate way to gauge uncertainty. Disagreement usually means lower confidence rather than one model being wrong.

entries.heading: Reading a forecast well
entries.source: WMO guidance on numerical weather prediction, public documentation
entries.text: Treat timing to within a few hours rather than to the minute, expect placement errors of tens of kilometres for convective rain, and pay attention to the probability and to the range between minimum and maximum values rather than to a single headline number.

entries.heading: Common weather terminology
entries.source: WMO International Meteorological Vocabulary and IMD public glossary
entries.text: > Source: WMO International Meteorological Vocabulary and IMD public glossary

entries.heading: Terms you will see in forecasts
entries.source: WMO International Meteorological Vocabulary and IMD public glossary
entries.text:
- Apparent temperature or "feels like": the temperature the body perceives, combining air temperature with humidity and wind.
- Probability of precipitation: the chance of at least 0.1 mm of rain at a point in a stated period.
- Scattered showers: brief rain affecting some places in an area, with dry gaps in between.
- Overcast: cloud covering essentially the whole sky.
- Squall: a sudden increase in wind speed of at least 30 km/h sustained for a few minutes.
- Gust: a brief peak in wind speed lasting seconds.
- Wind direction: always the direction the wind is coming from, so a westerly wind blows from west to east.
- Visibility: the greatest horizontal distance at which objects can be identified; below 1000 m is fog, 1000 m to 5000 m is mist or haze depending on humidity.
- Cloudburst: in Indian usage, rainfall of about 100 mm or more in one hour over a small area.

entries.heading: Watch, alert and warning
entries.source: WMO International Meteorological Vocabulary and IMD public glossary
entries.text: A watch means conditions are favourable for hazardous weather. An alert or advisory means hazardous weather is likely and preparation should begin. A warning means hazardous weather is occurring or imminent and protective action should be taken now. IMD also uses a colour code: green for no action, yellow for be aware, orange for be prepared, and red for take action.

entries.heading: Weather-related disaster preparedness
entries.source: National Disaster Management Authority (India) public preparedness guidance
entries.text: > Source: National Disaster Management Authority (India) public preparedness guidance

entries.heading: An emergency kit
entries.source: National Disaster Management Authority (India) public preparedness guidance
entries.text: Keep in one accessible bag: drinking water for three days, non-perishable food, essential medicines with prescriptions, a torch with spare batteries, a power bank, a first aid kit, a whistle, copies of identity documents in a waterproof pouch, some cash in small notes, and a battery or hand-crank radio.

entries.heading: A family plan
entries.source: National Disaster Management Authority (India) public preparedness guidance
entries.text: Agree on a meeting point, an out-of-area contact everyone can call, and who collects children from school. Save local emergency numbers, and note that 112 is the single emergency number in India. Practise the plan with everyone in the household, including the route to the nearest shelter or higher ground.

entries.heading: Before the season
entries.source: National Disaster Management Authority (India) public preparedness guidance
entries.text: Clear roof drains and gutters before the monsoon, check that trees near the building are pruned, repair loose roofing sheets and signage, and note whether your locality has a history of waterlogging. Keep insurance and property documents digitised.

entries.heading: Staying informed
entries.source: National Disaster Management Authority (India) public preparedness guidance
entries.text: Rely on official sources during an event: IMD bulletins and nowcasts, state disaster management authority advisories, district administration announcements and local radio. Automated app assessments, including this one, are useful for planning but do not replace an official warning.

entries.heading: Helping others
entries.source: National Disaster Management Authority (India) public preparedness guidance
entries.text: Check on elderly neighbours, people living alone, people with disabilities and outdoor workers before and during extreme weather. Most early rescue in Indian disasters is done by neighbours before formal agencies arrive.

entries.docTitle: Using weather information for everyday decisions
entries.heading: Using weather information for everyday decisions
entries.source: General public-safety guidance; thresholds stated here follow IMD and Beaufort classifications
entries.text: > Source: General public-safety guidance; thresholds stated here follow IMD and Beaufort classifications

entries.docTitle: Using weather information for everyday decisions
entries.heading: Should I carry an umbrella
entries.source: General public-safety guidance; thresholds stated here follow IMD and Beaufort classifications
entries.text: If the probability of precipitation is above about 40% at the time you will be outside, carrying rain protection is reasonable. Above 70%, plan for rain rather than hoping to avoid it. Check hourly values rather than the daily summary: a daily 60% may all sit in one evening window.

entries.docTitle: Using weather information for everyday decisions
entries.heading: Is it safe to travel
entries.source: General public-safety guidance; thresholds stated here follow IMD and Beaufort classifications
entries.text: Consider four things: rainfall intensity during your travel window, gust speed, visibility, and thunderstorm risk. Heavy rain reduces braking grip and visibility; gusts above about 60 km/h affect two-wheelers and high-sided vehicles; visibility below 500 m makes highway driving hazardous; and thunderstorms add lightning risk for anyone outdoors. If two or more of these apply, consider delaying the trip.

entries.docTitle: Using weather information for everyday decisions
entries.heading: Planning outdoor work or sport
entries.source: General public-safety guidance; thresholds stated here follow IMD and Beaufort classifications
entries.text: Schedule strenuous activity outside the 11:00 to 16:00 window on hot days, and check the UV index as well as the temperature. On days with afternoon thunderstorm potential, finish outdoor sessions before the usual convective peak in the late afternoon.

entries.docTitle: Using weather information for everyday decisions
entries.heading: Drying clothes, farming and events
entries.source: General public-safety guidance; thresholds stated here follow IMD and Beaufort classifications
entries.text: Look at the rainfall probability across consecutive hours, not the daily total, and at humidity, since high humidity slows drying even without rain. For events, gust speed matters for tents and stages, and thunderstorm probability matters for any gathering in the open.

entries.docTitle: Seasons and the monsoon in India
entries.heading: The four meteorological seasons
entries.source: India Meteorological Department seasonal definitions, public documentation
entries.text: IMD divides the year into winter (January to February), pre-monsoon or summer (March to May), the southwest monsoon (June to September), and the post-monsoon or northeast monsoon (October to December).

entries.docTitle: Seasons and the monsoon in India
entries.heading: Southwest monsoon
entries.source: India Meteorological Department seasonal definitions, public documentation
entries.text: The southwest monsoon normally reaches Kerala around 1 June and covers the country by mid-July, withdrawing from northwest India from mid-September. It delivers roughly three quarters of India's annual rainfall. Within the season, active spells with widespread rain alternate with break spells that can last a week or more.

entries.docTitle: Seasons and the monsoon in India
entries.heading: Northeast monsoon
entries.source: India Meteorological Department seasonal definitions, public documentation
entries.text: From October to December, retreating winds bring rainfall to Tamil Nadu, coastal Andhra Pradesh, Rayalaseema, south interior Karnataka and Kerala. For Tamil Nadu this is the main rainy season, and it coincides with the peak cyclone period in the Bay of Bengal.

entries.docTitle: Seasons and the monsoon in India
entries.heading: Pre-monsoon severe weather
entries.source: India Meteorological Department seasonal definitions, public documentation
entries.text: March to May brings intense surface heating, heatwaves over central and northern India, and localised severe thunderstorms with hail and squalls. In eastern India these are known as Nor'westers or Kalbaisakhi and can produce damaging wind gusts with little warning.

entries.docTitle: Seasons and the monsoon in India
entries.heading: Regional note: interior Karnataka
entries.source: India Meteorological Department seasonal definitions, public documentation
entries.text: Districts of interior Karnataka such as Ballari (Bellary) are semi-arid, with hot dry summers, moderate southwest monsoon rain and a secondary rainfall peak in September and October. Rainfall there is more variable year to year than on the coast, which makes the forecast probability more useful than any single seasonal average.
